name: Caffeine
notes: Pure caffeine powder is far more dangerous than drinks. The FDA says one teaspoon of powder equals roughly 28 cups of coffee, and it is almost impossible to measure safely at home. Symptoms of too much: racing heart, tremor, vomiting, seizures.
sources: FDA: Pure and highly concentrated caffeine

name: Table salt (sodium chloride)
notes: Salt poisoning is a real risk, especially in small children. Never use salt water to induce vomiting.

name: Alcohol (ethanol)
notes: Drinking fast can be dangerous at far lower amounts, and children are much more vulnerable. US guidance is up to 1 drink a day for women and 2 for men. Signs of alcohol poisoning: confusion, vomiting, slow or irregular breathing, passing out. Call 911.

name: Nutmeg
notes: Normal cooking amounts are fine. Poisoning has been reported around 5 g (about 2 teaspoons) or more: nausea, racing heart, confusion, hallucinations, lasting a day or longer. Deaths are rare and no firm lethal dose is established.
sources: Poison control center case reports on nutmeg ingestion

name: Sugar (sucrose)
lethalBasis: rat LD50; not a realistic human figure
notes: The lethal figure comes from rats. A person could not realistically eat that much, and the real harms of sugar are long-term, not a single-dose poisoning. Guidance limit shown is the American Heart Association figure for added sugar for women.
sources: Sucrose safety data sheet (rat oral LD50)

name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol, paracetamol)
notes: Accidental overdose is common because acetaminophen is hidden in many cold, flu and sleep products. Count every source. An overdose can feel fine for the first day while liver damage develops, so call Poison Control immediately if more than directed was taken.

name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)
notes: OTC label limit is 1,200 mg a day unless a doctor says otherwise. Take with food. Can harm the stomach and kidneys at higher doses. Call Poison Control if more than directed was taken.
